memorial_au_anzac_day.intro: Anzac Day on 25 April honours Australians and New Zealanders who served and died in wars, marking the 1915 Gallipoli landing.
memorial_au_anzac_day.history: On 25 April 1915 the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps (ANZAC) landed at Gallipoli in Ottoman Turkey during the First World War. The costly campaign became a defining national memory, and the date now commemorates all who served.
memorial_au_anzac_day.traditions: The day begins with solemn dawn services, followed by marches of veterans, the playing of the Last Post and the words "Lest we forget". People wear rosemary sprigs and play two-up, a traditional coin game.
funFacts: ANZAC stands for Australian and New Zealand Army Corps.
Dawn services recall the early-morning Gallipoli landing.
Two-up is an Anzac Day tradition. The conditions under which it is permitted depend on state rules.

memorial_ca_national_day_for_truth_and_r.intro: The National Day for Truth and Reconciliation on 30 September honours the children who were sent to residential schools and the survivors, families and communities affected. It has been a federal holiday since 2021.
memorial_ca_national_day_for_truth_and_r.history: For more than a century about 150,000 Indigenous children were taken to church-run residential schools, where many suffered abuse and thousands died. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission called for a day of remembrance in 2015, and Parliament created the holiday in 2021 after indications of possible unmarked burials were reported in Kamloops.
memorial_ca_national_day_for_truth_and_r.traditions: Canadians wear orange shirts, a custom started by survivor Phyllis Webstad, whose new orange shirt was taken from her on her first day at school. Communities hold walks, ceremonies and moments of silence, and buildings are lit in orange.
funFacts: The date was chosen because children were taken from their families in late September.
Orange Shirt Day began in Williams Lake, British Columbia, in 2013.
The message of the day is "Every Child Matters".
The last residential school closed in 1996.

memorial_ca_remembrance_day.intro: Remembrance Day on 11 November honours Canadians who served and died in war, symbolised by the red poppy.
memorial_ca_remembrance_day.history: 11 November recalls the 1918 armistice that ended the First World War. Canada, which lost more than 60,000 in that war, honours the fallen of all conflicts. The poppy comes from the poem ‚In Flanders Fields‘ by Canadian John McCrae.
memorial_ca_remembrance_day.traditions: At 11 a.m. Canadians observe two minutes of silence. The national ceremony at the National War Memorial in Ottawa features wreaths, the Last Post and a flypast, and millions wear poppies in the weeks before.
funFacts: ‚In Flanders Fields‘ was written by Canadian John McCrae in 1915.
Poppies are worn from late October until 11 November.
The Silver Cross Mother lays a wreath for all bereaved families.

memorial_fr_armistice_day.intro: 11 November marks the 1918 armistice that ended the First World War and honours all French soldiers who died for the country.
memorial_fr_armistice_day.history: At 11 a.m. on 11 November 1918 the armistice signed at Compiègne silenced the guns of the Western Front. France lost some 1.4 million soldiers. Since 1922 the date has been a national day of remembrance, later extended to the fallen of all wars.
memorial_fr_armistice_day.traditions: The President lays a wreath at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier beneath the Arc de Triomphe in Paris, where an eternal flame burns. Across the country, citizens and veterans gather at war memorials for a minute of silence.
funFacts: The armistice took effect at the 11th hour of the 11th day of the 11th month.
The eternal flame under the Arc de Triomphe is rekindled every evening since 1923.
The blue cornflower (le Bleuet) is France’s symbol of remembrance.

memorial_nz_anzac_day.intro: Anzac Day on 25 April honours New Zealanders and Australians who served and died in wars, marking the 1915 Gallipoli landing.
memorial_nz_anzac_day.history: On 25 April 1915 the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps (ANZAC) landed at Gallipoli during the First World War. For a young nation the heavy losses became a powerful symbol, and the day now remembers all New Zealanders who served.
memorial_nz_anzac_day.traditions: New Zealanders gather for dawn services at war memorials, followed by veterans’ parades, wreath-laying and the Last Post. Many wear red poppies, and returned-services clubs host commemorations.
funFacts: ANZAC stands for Australian and New Zealand Army Corps.
The red poppy is the symbol of remembrance.
Dawn services echo the dawn landing at Gallipoli in 1915.

memorial_us_memorial_day.intro: Memorial Day on the last Monday in May is the U.S. day of remembrance for fallen American soldiers. It is also the unofficial start of summer in the U.S.
memorial_us_memorial_day.history: The day grew out of the American Civil War (1861–1865), in which over 600,000 soldiers died. In May 1868 General John A. Logan ordered a ‘Decoration Day' on which the graves of fallen soldiers were to be decorated with flowers. The custom spread after both World Wars and today commemorates all U.S. soldiers who fell in war. In 1971 the day was officially moved to the last Monday in May — to create a long weekend.
memorial_us_memorial_day.traditions: At Arlington National Cemetery the President lays a wreath at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. Families visit graves, decorating them with flags and flowers. At 3 p.m. local time the ‘National Moment of Remembrance' calls for a moment of silence nationwide. There are also traditional parades, barbecues and the Indianapolis 500 motor race.
funFacts: Arlington National Cemetery is the resting place of service members, veterans and eligible family members, not only those killed in war.
The red poppy became a symbol of remembrance after World War I — inspired by the poem ‘In Flanders Fields'.
The first Indianapolis 500 took place on 30 May 1911. Today the race is traditionally part of Memorial Day weekend.
The older name ‘Decoration Day’ refers to decorating graves. The name ‘Memorial Day’ was already in use long before 1971.
